evidence.claim: The World Bank says Nigeria financed inefficient and regressive petrol, electricity, and foreign-exchange subsidies that benefited mainly wealthy households, cost more than education, health, and social protection spending in 2021, and crowded out pro-poor programs while revenue and spending stayed very low.
evidence.title: To Promote Inclusive and Sustainable Development, Nigeria Needs to Fix its Public Finances
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank says Nigeria financed inefficient and regressive petrol, electricity, and foreign-exchange subsidies that benefited mainly wealthy households, cost more than education, health, and social protection spending in 2021, and crowded out pro-poor programs while revenue and spending stayed very low.
evidence.source_locator: press release description and closing quote paragraphs
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary World Bank press release on the public-finance review with direct fiscal and distributional claims.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to the 2022 fiscal structure and policy choices available to Buhari.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to Buhari's fiscal authority, but also reflects inherited revenue structure and sectoral leakages.
contrary_evidence: The review evaluates a multi-year fiscal structure, so it is not a clean measure of one-year personal performance.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said gasoline subsidies would cost Nigeria roughly 5 trillion naira in 2022, mainly benefit richer households, and leave the country unable to benefit fiscally from high oil prices unless it adopted a single market-responsive exchange rate, removed the subsidy, and redirected resources toward investment and jobs.
evidence.title: A 'Business Unusual' approach, even more urgently needed to reduce inflation, lessen fiscal pressures, and attract investment for jobs
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said gasoline subsidies would cost Nigeria roughly 5 trillion naira in 2022, mainly benefit richer households, and leave the country unable to benefit fiscally from high oil prices unless it adopted a single market-responsive exchange rate, removed the subsidy, and redirected resources toward investment and jobs.
evidence.source_locator: press release body, subsidy and policy-priority paragraphs
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary World Bank policy note released during 2022 with explicit estimates and reform prescriptions.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 macro-policy context for Buhari's administration.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Administration-level attribution is fair for fiscal and exchange-rate choices, but oil prices and oil theft were not fully under Buhari's control.
contrary_evidence: The report is advisory and does not itself prove the government implemented the recommended reforms in 2022.

evidence.claim: By late 2022 the World Bank said Nigeria's economy was still held back by business-as-usual management, inflation had surged to 21.1 percent, as many as five million more Nigerians had been pushed into poverty, and the petrol subsidy was likely to exceed five trillion naira, while reforms were needed to restore macro stability, broaden private investment, and expand social protection.
evidence.title: To reduce its vulnerability to crisis and rise to its potential, Nigeria has urgent choices to make
evidence.excerpt: By late 2022 the World Bank said Nigeria's economy was still held back by business-as-usual management, inflation had surged to 21.1 percent, as many as five million more Nigerians had been pushed into poverty, and the petrol subsidy was likely to exceed five trillion naira, while reforms were needed to restore macro stability, broaden private investment, and expand social protection.
evidence.source_locator: press release body, opening summary and reform paragraphs
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary World Bank Nigeria Development Update press release with direct 2022 welfare and macro claims.
evidence.period_fit: Directly reports late-2022 conditions under Buhari's final year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partly attributable to Buhari's administration because the report ties the problems to fiscal and exchange-rate policy, but external shocks also matter.
contrary_evidence: The report also acknowledges external oil-price conditions, so not all deterioration is ruler-controlled.

evidence.claim: The IMF said higher oil prices created an opportunity to build fiscal space and FX reserves that was not harnessed, that fuel subsidies were a formidable drain on fiscal revenues, and that Nigeria needed tighter policy, stronger revenue mobilization, exchange-rate reform, and governance fixes including action on oil theft and leakages.
evidence.title: Nigeria: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2022 Article IV Mission
evidence.excerpt: The IMF said higher oil prices created an opportunity to build fiscal space and FX reserves that was not harnessed, that fuel subsidies were a formidable drain on fiscal revenues, and that Nigeria needed tighter policy, stronger revenue mobilization, exchange-rate reform, and governance fixes including action on oil theft and leakages.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary IMF mission statement written during the target year, with explicit fiscal and exchange-rate judgments.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 policy assessment of the Buhari administration.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Administration-level attribution is fair for fiscal, exchange-rate, and governance choices, though oil prices, theft, and security conditions are only partly attributable to Buhari.
contrary_evidence: The IMF notes positive growth in services and agriculture, so the economy was not uniformly contracting.

evidence.claim: The CBN's 2022 MPC decisions show a tightening cycle, with the Monetary Policy Rate raised from 11.5 percent to 13.0, then 14.0, 15.5, and 16.5 percent over the year.
evidence.title: Monetary Policy Decisions
evidence.excerpt: The CBN's 2022 MPC decisions show a tightening cycle, with the Monetary Policy Rate raised from 11.5 percent to 13.0, then 14.0, 15.5, and 16.5 percent over the year.
evidence.source_locator: 2022 decision entries on the page for May, July, September, and November 2022
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official central-bank policy record listing the 2022 rate decisions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect and partial; Buhari did not set rates personally, but he appointed the CBN leadership and oversaw the fiscal environment.
contrary_evidence: The same CBN record implies inflation and exchange-rate pressure were already severe, so tightening was reactive as well as corrective.

evidence.claim: Buhari signed the 2022 Appropriation Bill and 2021 Finance Bill into law, restoring a predictable January-to-December fiscal year, while asking for amendment and virement because the National Assembly had altered many projects and allocations.
evidence.title: President Buhari Signs N17.127tr 2022 Budget Into Law, Directs MDAs to Commence Early Preparation of 2023 Transition Budget
evidence.excerpt: Buhari signed the 2022 Appropriation Bill and 2021 Finance Bill into law, restoring a predictable January-to-December fiscal year, while asking for amendment and virement because the National Assembly had altered many projects and allocations.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct official record of the president's fiscal act and stated concerns about budget changes.
evidence.period_fit: Pre-2022 enactment that governed the 2022 fiscal framework.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct ruler action, though the resulting budget also reflects National Assembly amendments and inherited fiscal constraints.
contrary_evidence: The president said the enacted budget still needed amendment/virement, suggesting implementation friction rather than a clean policy win.

evidence.claim: Buhari framed the 2022 budget around conservative oil-price and exchange-rate assumptions, projected 4.2 percent growth and 13 percent inflation, and said the budget aimed at diversification, infrastructure, poverty reduction, and gender-responsive budgeting.
evidence.title: 2022 Budget Speech: Budget of Economic Growth and Sustainability – President Buhari
evidence.excerpt: Buhari framed the 2022 budget around conservative oil-price and exchange-rate assumptions, projected 4.2 percent growth and 13 percent inflation, and said the budget aimed at diversification, infrastructure, poverty reduction, and gender-responsive budgeting.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official budget speech directly states the administration's intended priorities, though it is self-presentational.
evidence.period_fit: Pre-2022 policy proposal that set the 2022 budget agenda.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct to Buhari as budget proposer, but it is intent rather than implementation.
contrary_evidence: The budget speech sets intentions; it does not establish whether the promised outcomes materialized in 2022.

evidence.claim: Buhari signed three bills on money laundering, terrorism prevention, and proceeds of crime, saying they were part of the administration's fight against corruption and illicit financing.
evidence.title: President Buhari Signs Three Bills Into Law
evidence.excerpt: Buhari signed three bills on money laundering, terrorism prevention, and proceeds of crime, saying they were part of the administration's fight against corruption and illicit financing.
evidence.source_locator: opening paragraph and presidential remarks on the new laws
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct official act with clear statutory content and anti-corruption purpose.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and relevant to governance conditions affecting economic performance.
contrary_evidence: Passing laws does not itself prove enforcement or reduced corruption in 2022.

evidence.claim: Buhari signed the National Health Insurance Authority Bill and said a fund would be created to cover 83 million poor Nigerians who cannot afford premiums, with a vulnerable-group fund and data systems to support implementation.
evidence.title: In Bid to Achieve Universal Coverage, President Buhari Signs National Health Authority Bill Into Law
evidence.excerpt: Buhari signed the National Health Insurance Authority Bill and said a fund would be created to cover 83 million poor Nigerians who cannot afford premiums, with a vulnerable-group fund and data systems to support implementation.
evidence.source_locator: opening paragraph and presidential remarks on the coverage fund
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct official act with explicit welfare-targeting language and named coverage figures.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct ruler action, though actual coverage depends on follow-through by health institutions and states.
contrary_evidence: Implementation and funding were not demonstrated by the signing alone.

evidence.claim: Buhari approved the appointment of Semiu Adeyemi Adeniran as NBS Statistician-General and CEO; the notice describes him as a professional statistician with more than three decades of experience and prior NBS leadership roles.
evidence.title: President Buhari Approves Appointment of Semiu Adeyemi Adeniran as Statistician-General of the Federation and Chief Executive Officer of the National Bureau of Statistics
evidence.excerpt: Buhari approved the appointment of Semiu Adeyemi Adeniran as NBS Statistician-General and CEO; the notice describes him as a professional statistician with more than three decades of experience and prior NBS leadership roles.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official appointment notice with a direct attribution and a specific technocratic résumé.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 appointment relevant to data capacity and evidence-based policy.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct ruler action, though one technocratic appointment does not prove the quality of the broader economic team.
contrary_evidence: A single technocratic appointment does not offset other evidence of politicization in economic offices.

evidence.claim: Buhari said cabinet selection had been careful to bring in the best and most competent people, that new members were added to inject fresh energies, skills, and ideas, and that replacements would be made without delay so governance would not suffer.
evidence.title: President Buhari's Speech at the Valedictory Session for Appointees Leaving the Cabinet to Pursue Political Ambition
evidence.excerpt: Buhari said cabinet selection had been careful to bring in the best and most competent people, that new members were added to inject fresh energies, skills, and ideas, and that replacements would be made without delay so governance would not suffer.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct official speech, but the competence claim is self-assessment rather than independent verification.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 statement about cabinet composition and governance continuity.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct ruler claim about his own appointments and cabinet management.
contrary_evidence: The speech is self-justifying and does not independently prove competence or depoliticization.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that ten cabinet ministers resigned to pursue election bids and that the government had asked ministers, ambassadors, agency heads, and other political appointees including the central bank governor to resign if they planned to join the 2023 race.
evidence.title: Ten Nigerian cabinet ministers resign to run in next year's election
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that ten cabinet ministers resigned to pursue election bids and that the government had asked ministers, ambassadors, agency heads, and other political appointees including the central bank governor to resign if they planned to join the 2023 race.
evidence.source_locator: opening paragraph and subsequent Reuters copy
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters reporting, but it is indirect and partly about political appointee rules rather than economic performance itself.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 evidence of politicization around key public offices.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly traces to Buhari's directive, though the resignations reflect the broader election cycle and not economic policy alone.
contrary_evidence: Buhari said replacements would be made quickly so governance would not suffer.

unresolved_gaps: No direct 2022 Buhari decision on nuclear brinkmanship, command-and-control, or other existential-risk use of presidential authority.
No independent audit of whether the 2021-2022 safeguards and physical-protection framework was actually implemented in practice.
No direct evidence of Buhari personally directing external military operations, proxy conduct, or coercive cross-border action in 2022.
No substantive mediation track or concrete ceasefire result led by Buhari himself.
Independent, case-level follow-through on prosecutions and investigations for major 2022 abuses is thin.
Some severe insecurity items are still better understood as state failure in a violent environment than as direct ruler-directed violence.
No independent pre-election audit of how fully the Electoral Act 2022 was implemented before the 2023 polls.
Much of the affirmative evidence is self-description from Buhari and his administration.
Budget execution and capital-spending delivery are not independently audited at the project level here.
Household-level and regional distributional causality remains only partially evidenced.
Independent audit evidence on how much of the announced welfare and health delivery actually reached beneficiaries in 2022 is limited.
The chapter still mixes federal action, donor support, and inherited deprivation.
No direct 2022 evidence of Buhari's assets, procurement benefits, bribes, or formal audit/court findings tied to personal enrichment.
The family-appointment case is strong on patronage but still thin on Buhari's knowledge, benefit, and intent beyond approval.
The Lake Chad arms claim is shown as unsupported, but there is no public correction or retraction by Buhari in the package.
Independent audit-grade evidence on the delivery tracker and the administration's correction of weak implementers is still limited.
The chapter still depends heavily on macro outcomes that mix Buhari-era policy with inherited constraints and external shocks.
